title: No stable accuracy gap between GROW and PRUNE on small multilayer perceptron benchmarks across compactness levels
content: On a 3-layer fully-connected network with two hidden layers of 256 units each (784→256→256→10, ReLU activation, unit masking on the two hidden layers), trained with SGD (learning rate η=0.01) for 5 structural-edit cycles with 20 epochs per cycle, the GROW method—which starts from 10% of the target active-unit count and iteratively activates units based on the fraction of post-activation values exceeding a threshold of 0.05 on a mini-batch, with no weight rewinding—and the PRUNE method—iterative magnitude pruning starting from 100% active units, pruning the lowest-scoring units by mean absolute weight magnitude, rewinding surviving weights to a rewind checkpoint after each pruning—produce closely matched winning-ticket final accuracy and winning-ticket trajectory-average accuracy across compactness budgets c∈{20,30,40,50}% (fraction of weights retained across growable and prunable layers) with no consistent ordering, on three benchmarks: (1) IID (independent and identically distributed) MNIST (10-class handwritten-digit classification, 60,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 28×28 grayscale), (2) class-incremental Split-MNIST (5 tasks of 2 classes each, shared 10-way classifier head, no task-identity routing, Tiny Experience Replay buffer storing 50 samples per class), and (3) the analogous Split-FashionMNIST setting. The winning-ticket evaluation freezes the final discovered mask, reinitializes the model weights, and retrains from scratch; trajectory-average accuracy is the mean cumulative test accuracy across the training trajectory. This demonstrates that the GROW-PRUNE asymmetry is not inherent to sparsity or class-incremental training regimes and only becomes visible in harder feature-learning settings.

title: GROW achieves higher Cycle-ACC than PRUNE on CIFAR-100 across all compactness levels with a dense convolutional trunk and masked fully-connected head
content: On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with a hybrid ConvNet consisting of a dense two-layer convolutional trunk (conv1: 3→32, k=3, p=1, ReLU, maxpool(2); conv2: 32→64, k=3, p=1, ReLU, maxpool(2); flatten to 4096) followed by a four-layer fully-connected head with unit-level masking (fc1: 4096→512, fc2: 512→512, fc3: 512→256, fc4: 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), trained with SGD (η=0.1) for 5 structural-edit cycles with 40 epochs per cycle, the GROW method—which starts from 10% of the target active-unit count and iteratively activates units using an activation-frequency heuristic (fraction of post-activation values exceeding τ=0.05) with no weight rewinding—achieves higher Cycle-ACC (test accuracy at the end of each structural-edit cycle during the GROW procedure) than PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning starting from 100% active units, rewinding surviving weights after each pruning) at every compactness level c∈{20,30,40,50}% (e.g., at c=50%: GROW 54.338±0.221 vs. PRUNE 50.227±0.548; Welch t-test p < 0.001 at all compactness levels), with the gap increasing at higher compactness.

title: No GROW winning-ticket advantage over PRUNE on CIFAR-100 with ConvNet after retraining final masks from scratch
content: On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk: conv1 3→32, conv2 32→64, maxpool, flatten to 4096; four-layer fully-connected masked head: fc1 4096→512, fc2 512→512, fc3 512→256, fc4 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), after freezing the final mask discovered by each method (GROW: activation-frequency-based unit activation from 10% active to target compactness, no rewind; PRUNE: iterative magnitude pruning from 100% active to target compactness with weight rewinding), reinitializing the model weights, and retraining from scratch (Winning-Ticket evaluation following the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis protocol), GROW and PRUNE produce similar final accuracy across compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}% (e.g., at c=20%: GROW 52.055±0.324 vs. PRUNE 52.057±0.283; at c=50%: GROW 50.260±0.257 vs. PRUNE 50.320±0.415; p > 0.05 at all compactness levels), with PRUNE slightly stronger at 40–50% compactness; the GROW Cycle-ACC advantage observed during structural editing does not translate to clearly superior retrainable sparse architectures.

title: PRUNE achieves higher Cycle-TAA than GROW on CIFAR-100 while Winning-Ticket TAA differences are not significant
content: On CIFAR-100 (100-class classification, 50,000 training images, 10,000 test images, 32×32 color images) with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk: conv1 3→32, conv2 32→64, maxpool, flatten to 4096; four-layer fully-connected masked head: fc1 4096→512, fc2 512→512, fc3 512→256, fc4 256→100, ReLU, unit masking on fc1-fc3), PRUNE achieves higher Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy, the mean test accuracy across all structural-edit checkpoints during the pruning procedure) than GROW (activation-frequency-based unit activation from 10% active to target compactness, no rewind) at low and intermediate compactness: at c=20% (PRUNE 48.519±0.348 vs. GROW 47.288±0.269, p < 0.001), c=30% (PRUNE 48.732±0.358 vs. GROW 47.871±0.374, p=0.0014), and c=40% (PRUNE 48.869±0.251 vs. GROW 48.338±0.291, p=0.0059), while at c=50% the two methods are nearly tied (PRUNE 48.997±0.240 vs. GROW 48.990±0.245, p=0.9637). Under Winning-Ticket retraining (freezing final mask, reinitializing weights, retraining from scratch), TAA differences between GROW and PRUNE are not statistically significant at any compactness (p > 0.05), further confirming that the GROW-PRUNE separation lies in adaptive dynamics rather than final architecture quality.

title: Newborn GROW units are forward-active but backward-starved at birth on CIFAR-100
content: On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), event-aligned cohort diagnostics computed on a single mini-batch at the moment of growth show that newborn units (units just activated by the GROW method) exhibit positive activation log-parity relative to incumbent units (units already active before growth), indicating forward participation, where log-parity is the natural logarithm of the ratio of mean per-unit activation rate (fraction of post-activation values exceeding a threshold τ on the mini-batch) for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units. Newborn units also exhibit strongly negative gradient log-parity (log ratio < 0), where gradient log-parity is the natural logarithm of the ratio of mean per-unit gradient magnitude (mean absolute pre-activation gradient |∂L/∂z_j| on the mini-batch) for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units. This demonstrates that the growth bottleneck is a backward-pass integration problem rather than a dead-unit problem—newborn units are not silent, but the current loss is less sensitive to changes through their downstream pathways.

title: Backward-signal disadvantage for newborn GROW units persists throughout training cycle on CIFAR-100
content: On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), post-birth dynamics tracked over the training segment remaining after each growth event (within the same cycle) show that newborn GROW units' activation ratio (mean per-unit activation rate of newborn units divided by that of incumbent units, measured on a mini-batch) approaches or exceeds parity (ratio close to or above 1), but their gradient ratio (mean per-unit gradient magnitude |∂L/∂z_j| of newborn units divided by that of incumbent units, measured on a mini-batch) remains far below parity (ratio < 1) throughout the entire cycle, including at the end-of-cycle checkpoint. This indicates that the backward-signal disadvantage is not merely a transient birth-time effect but persists over the available training horizon and limits how quickly newborn units can become useful.

title: Early integration parity correlates with Cycle-TAA across compactness levels and interventions on CIFAR-100
content: On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), across all compactness levels c∈{20,30,40,50}% and intervention methods (vanilla GROW, Two-Speed—temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters, Moment Transplant—copying optimizer buffers from a donor incumbent unit to newborn unit at birth, GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection of inactive units, Rand. Smooth-Leaky—a smoother randomized leaky activation function, Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by duplicating incumbent units), early gradient parity (mean natural logarithm of the ratio of per-unit gradient magnitude |∂L/∂z_j| for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units, averaged over the early post-birth training window) has a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.88 with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure), and early activation parity (mean natural logarithm of the ratio of per-unit activation rate for newborn units divided by that for incumbent units, averaged over the same window) has a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.83 with Cycle-TAA. This establishes a strong quantitative link between the degree of newborn integration during early post-insertion training and the resulting trajectory-average adaptive performance, supporting that backward credit assignment is the primary newborn-integration bottleneck.

title: GradMax and Rand. Smooth-Leaky best improve Cycle-TAA on CIFAR-100 among evaluated interventions
content: On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), among the evaluated interventions targeting the newborn integration bottleneck—Two-Speed (temporary learning-rate multiplier r>1 on newborn-associated parameters during warmup), Moment Transplant (copying optimizer buffers from a donor incumbent unit to newborn at birth), GradMax (gradient-based top-k selection of inactive units), Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function), and Net2Wider (function-preserving widening by duplicating selected incumbent units and redistributing outgoing weights)—GradMax-style gradient-based selection and Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation achieve the highest early integration parity (mean log-ratio of newborn-to-incumbent gradient magnitude and activation rate averaged over the early post-birth window) and the highest Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure), while Two-Speed and Net2Wider provide weaker or less consistent relief across compactness levels. This demonstrates that improving the integration of newborn units can strengthen adaptive-process performance, with selection policy and activation-level trainability being the most effective levers among those tested.

title: Edit-time integration improvement does not guarantee better retrained final masks on CIFAR-100
content: On CIFAR-100 with the same hybrid ConvNet (dense two-layer convolutional trunk and four-layer fully-connected masked head), retrained-mask winning-ticket accuracy (accuracy after freezing the final mask, reinitializing model weights, and retraining from scratch) is not monotonically aligned with Cycle-TAA (trajectory-average accuracy during the structural-edit procedure) across intervention methods (vanilla GROW, Two-Speed, Moment Transplant, GradMax, Rand. Smooth-Leaky, Net2Wider). Methods that substantially improve edit-time integration (such as GradMax or Rand. Smooth-Leaky) do not necessarily produce better final retrainable subnetworks, as shown by the lack of monotonic alignment in the Cycle-TAA vs. winning-ticket accuracy comparison across interventions. This decoupling shows that improved edit-time dynamics and final architecture quality are distinct objectives that may require separate optimization criteria.

title: GROW with Rand. Smooth-Leaky outperforms all methods on sequential accumulation of classes on Split-CIFAR100
content: On class-incremental Split-CIFAR100 (CIFAR-100 partitioned into 10 tasks of 10 classes each, shared 100-way classifier head, no task-identity routing at test time, known task boundaries, fixed per-task training budget, structural edits at task boundaries separated by substantial optimization time), GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky activation (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) outperforms DENSE (full-capacity training without structural editing), PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding), and all other growth variants (vanilla GROW, GROW+TwoSpeed—temporary learning-rate multiplier on newborn parameters, GROW+MomentTransplant—copying optimizer buffers from donor to newborn, GROW+GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection, GROW+Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by unit duplication) in final accuracy. This demonstrates that growth can be a competitive alternative to pruning in continual learning settings when newborn units have enough optimization time to integrate and are made more trainable through activation-level intervention.

title: PRUNE reliable under rapid shift while GROW with Rand. Smooth-Leaky is the most robust growth variant across plasticity-stressing continual learning benchmarks
content: Across five repeated-shift plasticity-stressing continual learning benchmarks—(1) Permuted MNIST (500 tasks, 10,000 images/task, fixed random pixel permutation per task, 1 epoch per task), (2) Random Label MNIST (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), (3) Random Label CIFAR (50 tasks, 1,200 fixed CIFAR-10 images/task, fresh random labels per task, 400 epochs per task), (4) 5+1 CIFAR (15 alternating hard/easy tasks from CIFAR-100, 780 update steps per task, classes do not repeat), and (5) Continual ImageNet (500 binary classification tasks, 1,200 images/task from ImageNet downsampled to 32×32, classes do not repeat, 10 epochs per task)—PRUNE (iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding) is the strongest or near-strongest structural baseline (compared against DENSE and GROW-family methods) in settings with rapid distribution change, consistent with the advantage of preserving mature capacity. Among growth-family methods, GROW combined with Rand. Smooth-Leaky (a smoother randomized leaky activation function) is the most robust growth variant—it consistently improves over vanilla GROW, narrows the gap to PRUNE, and is the only growth variant that becomes competitive with or outperforms PRUNE in settings where structural events are separated by more optimization time (Split-CIFAR100), while other birth interventions (Two-Speed—temporary learning-rate multiplier on newborn parameters, Moment Transplant—copying optimizer buffers from donor to newborn, GradMax—gradient-based top-k selection, Net2Wider—function-preserving widening by unit duplication) provide less consistent gains across this benchmark suite.
